content: Contact sampling should be conducted for children, particularly those under the age of five, who have been in contact with an Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) case within one week prior to or two weeks after the onset of paralysis. Examples of such contacts include siblings, other children living in the same household, or neighboring houses, as well as those who played with the AFP case during the relevant period. Stool specimens from these contacts may be collected for up to 60 days following the onset of paralysis, as poliovirus can be excreted for up to two months or longer. These specimens are typically collected from the community where the AFP case resides. However, if the AFP case stayed elsewhere during the critical time frame, specimen collection from contacts in those locations may also be necessary. Contact sampling is an integral part of routine AFP surveillance activities, especially in high-risk countries. It is particularly warranted in the following situations: when stool specimens from AFP cases are inadequate (e.g., specimens arriving at the laboratory in poor condition), when AFP cases reside in areas that are difficult to access or have compromised security, when hot AFP cases are identified, or when there are concerns about the collection or handling of the index AFP stool specimens. A hot case is defined as an AFP case exhibiting rapid progression of paralysis, asymmetrical paralysis, and fever at onset. Additional criteria may include being under five years of age, having received fewer than three doses of polio-containing vaccine or having an unknown vaccination status, and having visited areas or been in contact with groups where the virus has recently circulated. Laboratories must prioritize the processing of specimens from hot cases. The procedures for collecting and transporting contact specimens are identical to those for AFP cases. Each specimen must be clearly labeled as a contact specimen and include the EPID number of the AFP case (e.g., C1, C2, or C3). In outbreak situations, contact sampling may be expanded to enhance AFP surveillance. National surveillance and laboratory personnel must collaborate closely to implement this expansion. Efforts should be made to sample contacts of all AFP cases in outbreak-affected countries to improve virus detection. Sampling should also include contacts of AFP cases detected outside the subnational outbreak zone to monitor potential virus movement beyond the designated area. However, results from AFP contact sampling cannot confirm community-wide poliovirus transmission. Stool specimens should not be collected from contacts of individuals classified as WPV, aVDPV, cVDPV, unclassified VDPV, polio-compatible, or SL2-positive, nor from poliovirus-positive individuals or healthy children. All AFP case specimens must be processed in WHO-accredited laboratories within the Global Polio Laboratory Network (GPLN). These laboratories follow standardized protocols to isolate poliovirus, conduct intratypic differentiation, and perform genomic sequencing. Laboratory confirmation is based on the isolation of poliovirus in tissue culture cell monolayers (RD and L20B). Non-polio enterovirus (NPEV) isolation may also occur during testing, and these results must be reported separately. Intratypic differentiation is performed using reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to identify whether the virus is WPV, VDPV, or Sabin-like, as well as its serotype (1, 2, or 3). Genetic sequencing is used to track poliovirus transmission pathways by comparing the nucleotide sequence of the VP1-coding region of isolates. Laboratories must maintain accurate records for each sample using the EPID number to link epidemiological and laboratory data for each case. Results must be reported to the national program and WHO. A 60-day follow-up examination is conducted for certain AFP cases between the 60th and 90th day after paralysis onset to determine the presence of residual paralysis. If residual paralysis is observed, it provides further evidence that poliovirus is the likely cause. Follow-up should not occur before the 60th day, as paralysis may still resolve, leading to false-positive outcomes. AFP cases requiring 60-day follow-up include those with inadequate stool specimens, cases where WPV/VDPV has been isolated, and cases where Sabin-type poliovirus or nOPV2 has been isolated. During the follow-up, investigators must verify developments with the family, confirm the accuracy of the case investigation form, clinically assess the child, and complete the 60-day follow-up form, which should be submitted to the national surveillance unit. Procedures must be in place to ensure that AFP cases presenting in districts other than their district of residence are properly evaluated and that health staff in the relevant districts are promptly notified. For AFP cases from other countries, local and regional WHO offices should be informed. AFP cases are classified based on virological findings. If stool samples are inadequate and the patient has residual paralysis, is lost to follow-up, or has died by the time of the 60-day follow-up, the case is classified by a national expert review committee (ERC). The ERC may request additional clinical and hospital documentation to determine whether the case is compatible with poliomyelitis or should be discarded. Confirmed cases are those where WPV or VDPV has been isolated from stool specimens of the patient or their close contacts. Compatible cases are those without adequate specimens, where WPV or VDPV has not been isolated, but residual paralysis is present after 60 days, and the ERC deems the case clinically and epidemiologically consistent with poliomyelitis. Discarded cases are those adequately investigated with no laboratory evidence of WPV or VDPV infection, or where weakness resolves within 60 days, and the ERC determines the case is not compatible with poliomyelitis. A robust information system is essential for a successful polio eradication program. Surveillance data should be reviewed weekly at national, state, and district levels to monitor disease occurrence, assess changing patterns, evaluate risks, and track the progress of eradication efforts. Key indicators, such as the non-polio AFP rate and stool adequacy, must be regularly assessed to ensure the surveillance system functions effectively. Timeliness of detection, notification, investigation, and sample collection is critical to minimizing delays in identifying poliovirus transmission and responding to outbreaks. Regular analyses should be conducted to identify bottlenecks and address delays in the surveillance process.
